source: In larval forewings, the Hox chromatin conformation landscape consists of three well-delimited TADs, the first one spanning proboscipedia (pb) to Sex comb reduced (Scr), the second one around Antp, and the third one Ubx, abd-A, and Abd-B (Figures 2 and 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: A Boundary Element (BE) was robustly called at the region separating the Antp and Ubx TADs, situated in the Ubx last intron.
source: A Boundary Element (BE), was robustly called (see Materials and methods) at the region separating the Antp and Ubx TADs, situated in the Ubx last intron.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 2.

claim: Four CTCF binding sites were identified in a 1 kb interval within Antp-Ubx_BE, two of which were found in a tightly linked, convergent orientation.
source: A binding motif analysis identified 4 CTCF binding sites in a 1 kb interval within Antp-Ubx_BE, two of which were found in a tightly linked, convergent orientation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with TAD insulating role in mediating chromatin loop-extrusion (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by binding motif analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The convergent orientation of CTCF binding sites is consistent with TAD insulating role in mediating chromatin loop-extrusion.
source: A binding motif analysis identified 4 CTCF binding sites in a 1 kb interval within Antp-Ubx_BE, two of which were found in a tightly linked, convergent orientation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which is consistent with TAD insulating role in mediating chromatin loop-extrusion (Guo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about CTCF function supported by a citation.

claim: The concordance between Hi-C profiling and CTCF motif prediction suggests that Antp-Ubx_BE region might function as an insulator between regulatory domains of Antp and Ubx.
source: This concordance between Hi-C profiling and CTCF motif prediction thus suggests that Antp-Ubx_BE region might function as an insulator between regulatory domains of Antp and Ubx.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on Hi-C and CTCF motif data.

claim: Chromatin opening along the Antp/Ubx/abd-A interval is partitioned into several regions showing a transition of T2 to T3 activity.
source: These data reveal that chromatin opening along the Antp/Ubx/abd-A interval is partitioned into several regions showing a transition of T2 to T3 activity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: From the anterior to posterior Hox collinear order, chromatin-opening forms a block of forewing-enriched activity close to Antp and its 5' region.
source: From the anterior to posterior Hox collinear order (i.e. from Antp towards abd-A), chromatin-opening forms a block of forewing-enriched activity close to Antp and its 5' region, to a block of activity in both forewings and hindwings that stops at the Antp-Ubx_BE.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: A block of chromatin activity in both forewings and hindwings stops at the Antp-Ubx_BE.
source: From the anterior to posterior Hox collinear order (i.e. from Antp towards abd-A), chromatin-opening forms a block of forewing-enriched activity close to Antp and its 5' region, to a block of activity in both forewings and hindwings that stops at the Antp-Ubx_BE.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The region including Ubx and a large upstream region is strongly enriched for hindwing opening.
source: From Antp-Ubx_BE, the interval including Ubx and a large upstream region is strongly enriched for hindwing opening, consistently with previous studies that found it to be the only genomic region showing this pattern (Lewis et al., 2019; van der Burg et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 2B and previous studies.

claim: The region surrounding abd-A is devoid of differential open-chromatin activity between forewings and hindwings.
source: Last, the region surrounding abd-A is devoid of differential open-chromatin activity between forewings and hindwings, in accordance with the exclusion of its expression from thoracic segments (Warren et al., 1994; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: abd-A expression is excluded from thoracic segments.
source: Last, the region surrounding abd-A is devoid of differential open-chromatin activity between forewings and hindwings, in accordance with the exclusion of its expression from thoracic segments (Warren et al., 1994; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In pupal hindwings, the TAD spanning from proboscipedia (pb) to fushi-tarazu (ftz) faded in intensity compared to larval forewings.
source: We found two main differences in this contact landscape compared to the larval forewing (Figure 3). First, the TAD spanning from proboscipedia (pb) to fushi-tarazu (ftz) faded in intensity, while in contrast, the TAD around Antp remained strongly organized.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pupal hindwings, the TAD around Antp remained strongly organized.
source: We found two main differences in this contact landscape compared to the larval forewing (Figure 3). First, the TAD spanning from proboscipedia (pb) to fushi-tarazu (ftz) faded in intensity, while in contrast, the TAD around Antp remained strongly organized.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pupal hindwings, Ubx lost its physical association to the abd-A and Abd-B domains.
source: Second, Ubx lost its physical association to the abd-A and Abd-B domains, and gained a TAD boundary situated in the Ubx-AS5' intron.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pupal hindwings, Ubx gained a TAD boundary situated in the Ubx-AS5' intron.
source: Second, Ubx lost its physical association to the abd-A and Abd-B domains, and gained a TAD boundary situated in the Ubx-AS5' intron.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The differences in chromatin conformation between larval forewings and pupal hindwings may be due to chromatin remodeling between stages.
source: Specifically, these differences we observed may be due to chromatin remodeling between stages, as somewhat expected during metamorphosis (Gutierrez-Perez et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences and established knowledge about metamorphosis.

claim: It is possible hindwing development requires Ubx to be insulated from the more posterior enhancers.
source: Alternatively, it is also possible hindwing development requires Ubx to be insulated from the more posterior enhancers.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in TAD organization.

claim: The later hindwing sample showed a maintenance of Antp-Ubx separation.
source: Nonetheless the later hindwing sample showed a maintenance of Antp-Ubx separation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pupal hindwings, Ubx formed a smaller TAD spanning its coding exons 1–2.
source: First, while Ubx formed a smaller TAD spanning its coding exons 1–2, this region conserved a domain of hindwing-enriched open-chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: In pupal hindwings, the Ubx region conserved a domain of hindwing-enriched open-chromatin.
source: First, while Ubx formed a smaller TAD spanning its coding exons 1–2, this region conserved a domain of hindwing-enriched open-chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C and ATAC-seq data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: Boundary prediction called two possible, tightly linked TAD limits in the Antp-Ubx_BE region in pupal hindwings.
source: Second, boundary prediction called two possible, tightly linked TAD limits in the Antp-Ubx_BE region, showing that the last intron of Ubx still acts as an insulating region.
evidence: This claim is supported by Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The last intron of Ubx still acts as an insulating region in pupal hindwings.
source: Second, boundary prediction called two possible, tightly linked TAD limits in the Antp-Ubx_BE region, showing that the last intron of Ubx still acts as an insulating region.
evidence: This is an inference based on Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The Antp-Ubx_BE is relatively stable across two stages and wing serial homologs.
source: In conclusion, our preliminary comparison of Hox 3D conformation indicates that the Antp-Ubx_BE is relatively stable across two stages and wing serial homologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on Hi-C data analysis presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak in the inferred boundary interval might mediate the binding of insulator proteins.
source: Next, we reasoned that the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak present in the inferred boundary interval (Figure 4A) might mediate the binding of insulator proteins (Savitsky et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), or act as a transcriptional silencer (Segert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on ATAC-seq data and established knowledge about insulator proteins.

claim: The forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak in the inferred boundary interval might act as a transcriptional silencer.
source: Next, we reasoned that the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak present in the inferred boundary interval (Figure 4A) might mediate the binding of insulator proteins (Savitsky et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), or act as a transcriptional silencer (Segert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on ATAC-seq data and established knowledge about transcriptional silencers.

claim: The only forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak across a 150 kb region coincides with the midpoint between the two tentative hicFindTADs boundary predictions.
source: First, the only forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak across a 150 kb region (spanning the Ubx gene and the Antp-Ubx intergenic region), coincides with the midpoint between the two tentative hicFindTADs boundary predictions inferred from HiC data (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq and Hi-C data analysis presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Eight predicted binding-sites for the Drosophila CCCTC-Binding Factor (CTCF) are clustered in a 5 kb region around the differentially accessible region.
source: Second, during motif scans conducted across that 150 kb region we found eight predicted binding-sites for the Drosophila CCCTC-Binding Factor (CTCF) clustered in a 5 kb region around the differentially accessible region, and none elsewhere in the last Ubx intron (Figure 4A), suggesting the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak may function as a transcriptional insulator (Gambetta and Furlong, 2018; Postika et al., 2018; Kyrchanova et al., 2020; Kaushal et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif scanning analysis presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak may function as a transcriptional insulator.
source: Second, during motif scans conducted across that 150 kb region we found eight predicted binding-sites for the Drosophila CCCTC-Binding Factor (CTCF) clustered in a 5 kb region around the differentially accessible region, and none elsewhere in the last Ubx intron (Figure 4A), suggesting the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak may function as a transcriptional insulator (Gambetta and Furlong, 2018; Postika et al., 2018; Kyrchanova et al., 2020; Kaushal et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on CTCF motif analysis and established knowledge about insulators.

claim: The two candidate CTCF binding motifs within the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak are conserved across Lepidoptera and Trichoptera.
source: Last, the two candidate CTCF binding motifs that are within the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak are also conserved across Lepidoptera and Trichoptera (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), two lineages that diverged around 300 Mya (Jusino et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic conservation analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lepidoptera and Trichoptera diverged around 300 Mya.
source: Last, the two candidate CTCF binding motifs that are within the forewing-enriched ATAC-seq peak are also conserved across Lepidoptera and Trichoptera (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), two lineages that diverged around 300 Mya (Jusino et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CRISPR mutagenesis of the Antp-Ubx_BE target induced G0 mutants with homeotic transformations of their forewings into hindwings.
source: Remarkably, CRISPR mutagenesis of the Antp-Ubx_BE target induced G0 mutants with homeotic transformations of their forewings into hindwings (Figure 4B–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), including identity shifts in patterns, venation, and wing shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figures 4B–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Antp-Ubx_BE crispants showed homeotic transformations including identity shifts in patterns, venation, and wing shape.
source: Remarkably, CRISPR mutagenesis of the Antp-Ubx_BE target induced G0 mutants with homeotic transformations of their forewings into hindwings (Figure 4B–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), including identity shifts in patterns, venation, and wing shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figures 4B–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the Antp-Ubx_BE crispants showed hindwing effects.
source: It is important to note that none of the resulting crispants showed hindwing effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: Forewing homeotic phenotypes in Antp-Ubx_BE crispants can be attributed to indel mutations restricted to the intronic region, without disruption of the Ubx transcript.
source: Thus, we can reasonably attribute forewing homeotic phenotypes to indel mutations restricted to the intronic region, without disruption of the Ubx transcript, as this would result in hindwing phenotypes (Matsuoka and Monteiro, 2021; Tendolkar et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of hindwing phenotypes and established knowledge about Ubx function.

claim: Homeotic clones are first visible in Antp-Ubx_BE crispants at the pupal stage, with streaks of thinner cuticle.
source: Homeotic clones are first visible in Antp-Ubx_BE crispants at the pupal stage, with streaks of thinner cuticle, sometimes associated with local necrosis or with suture defects in the ventral midline, in particular where leg and wing pouches adjoin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of pupal phenotypes presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutant forewings of Antp-Ubx_BE crispants show streaks of more transparent wing epithelium when dissected out of the pupa.
source: When dissected out of the pupa, these mutant forewings also show streaks of more transparent wing epithelium, concomitantly with the territories of thinner cuticle above, and PCR genotyping of affected pupal wing tissue confirmed the presence of CRISPR-induced mutations at the Antp-Ubx_BE target site (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations and genotyping presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: PCR genotyping of affected pupal wing tissue confirmed the presence of CRISPR-induced mutations at the Antp-Ubx_BE target site.
source: When dissected out of the pupa, these mutant forewings also show streaks of more transparent wing epithelium, concomitantly with the territories of thinner cuticle above, and PCR genotyping of affected pupal wing tissue confirmed the presence of CRISPR-induced mutations at the Antp-Ubx_BE target site (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Color pattern homeotic clones in Antp-Ubx_BE crispants were salient at the adult stage.
source: Color pattern homeotic clones were salient at the adult stage, with for example, clonal losses of the forewing specific white-band, and partial acquisitions of the large M1-M2 hindwing eyespot.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of adult phenotypes presented in Figure 4.

claim: In one Antp-Ubx_BE crispant specimen, an ectopic, partial M1-M2 hindwing eyespot appeared in the R5-M1 region.
source: In one specimen, an ectopic, partial M1-M2 hindwing eyespot appeared in the R5-M1 region, suggesting a perturbation of the eyespot induction process in this wing.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of adult phenotypes presented in Figure 4.

claim: Nymphalid forewings have five radial veins (R1-5), which provide sturdiness for flight.
source: Nymphalid forewings have five radial veins (R1-5), which provide sturdiness for flight (Wootton, 1993), while hindwings have only two Radial veins.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Nymphalid hindwings have only two Radial veins.
source: Nymphalid forewings have five radial veins (R1-5), which provide sturdiness for flight (Wootton, 1993), while hindwings have only two Radial veins.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Forewing homeotic mutants of Antp-Ubx_BE crispants showed mosaic venation defects in the Radial vein area.
source: Forewing homeotic mutants showed mosaic venation defects in the Radial vein area (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of adult phenotypes presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Higher expressivity mutant forewings of Antp-Ubx_BE crispants were smaller and rounder, reminiscent of hindwing shape.
source: Finally, higher expressivity mutant forewings were smaller and rounder, reminiscent of hindwing shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of adult phenotypes presented in Figure 4.

claim: Antp-Ubx_BE crispants showed forewing clones with strong ectopic expression of Ubd-A.
source: Crispants showed forewing clones with strong ectopic expression of Ubd-A (Figure 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data presented in Figures 4D–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Antp-Ubx_BE forewing homeoses are due to the de-repression of Ubx in forewing tissue.
source: This result supports the inference that Antp-Ubx_BE forewing homeoses are due to the de-repression of Ubx in this tissue.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ectopic Ubd-A expression observed in forewing clones.

claim: Mutagenesis of the Ubx-IT1 first exon in J. coenia resulted in crispants with small homeotic phenotypes in forewings and hindwings.
source: Mutagenesis of the Ubx-IT1 first exon in J. coenia, and of the Ubx-IT1 promoter in V. cardui, both resulted in crispants with small homeotic phenotypes in forewings and hindwings (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutagenesis of the Ubx-IT1 promoter in V. cardui resulted in crispants with small homeotic phenotypes in forewings and hindwings.
source: Mutagenesis of the Ubx-IT1 first exon in J. coenia, and of the Ubx-IT1 promoter in V. cardui, both resulted in crispants with small homeotic phenotypes in forewings and hindwings (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ubx-IT1 crispants were obtained at a rate of 11 out of 236 adults.
source: Given the scarcity of Ubx-IT1 crispants obtained (11 out of 236 adults), and the small size of the homeotic clones within them, we infer the occasional phenotypes may be due to rare alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data summarized in Figure 9 and Table 1.

claim: The occasional phenotypes in Ubx-IT1 crispants may be due to rare alleles.
source: Given the scarcity of Ubx-IT1 crispants obtained (11 out of 236 adults), and the small size of the homeotic clones within them, we infer the occasional phenotypes may be due to rare alleles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low frequency and small size of homeotic clones.

claim: The homeotic phenotypes in Ubx-IT1 crispants may reflect the effects of regulatory perturbation on Ubx itself.
source: Thus, rather than evidence of functionality of the Ubx-IT1 transcript, the homeotic phenotypes may rather reflect the effects of regulatory perturbation on Ubx itself, with some random mutations in this intronic region resulting in hindwing Ubx loss-of-function, and some others triggering derepression in forewings.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the bidirectional homeotic phenotypes observed.

claim: Mutagenesis of the first exon of Ubx-AS5' resulted in twelve hindwing mutants and a single forewing mutant.
source: Likewise, next we mutagenized the first exon of Ubx-AS5', located upstream of the Ubx promoter, and obtained twelve hindwing mutants and a single forewing mutant (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The results of Ubx-AS5' CRISPR experiments may be explained by regulatory disruption of Ubx transcription.
source: As with Ubx-IT1 CRISPR experiments, these results may be explained by regulatory disruption of Ubx transcription, with a higher ratio of hindwing phenotypes compared to forewings linked to the proximity of the Ubx promoter.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the phenotypic data and proximity to the Ubx promoter.

claim: The mutational interrogation at Ubx-IT1 and Ubx-AS5' loci can result in dual loss (hindwing) and gain (forewing) of Ubx function effects.
source: Overall, we conclude that the mutational interrogation at these loci can result in dual loss (hindwing) and gain (forewing) of Ubx function effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the CRISPR mutagenesis experiments at these loci.

claim: All CRISPR targets yielded homeotic phenotypes.
source: All CRISPR targets yielded homeotic phenotypes (Figure 9), with two kinds of interference with Ubx expression – forewing gain-of-function effects, and hindwing loss-of-function effects – and indicating the presence of regulatory sequences (broadly defined), that repress or enhance Ubx expression in this region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the summary of CRISPR experiments presented in Figure 9.

claim: CRISPR targets showed two kinds of interference with Ubx expression: forewing gain-of-function effects, and hindwing loss-of-function effects.
source: All CRISPR targets yielded homeotic phenotypes (Figure 9), with two kinds of interference with Ubx expression – forewing gain-of-function effects, and hindwing loss-of-function effects – and indicating the presence of regulatory sequences (broadly defined), that repress or enhance Ubx expression in this region.
evidence: This claim is supported by the summary of CRISPR experiments presented in Figure 9.

claim: The CRISPR results indicate the presence of regulatory sequences that repress or enhance Ubx expression in this region.
source: All CRISPR targets yielded homeotic phenotypes (Figure 9), with two kinds of interference with Ubx expression – forewing gain-of-function effects, and hindwing loss-of-function effects – and indicating the presence of regulatory sequences (broadly defined), that repress or enhance Ubx expression in this region.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CRISPR mutagenesis results.

claim: Butterfly CRISPR experiments generate random mutations by non-homologous end joining repair, that are usually deletions.
source: In essence, butterfly CRISPR experiments generate random mutations by non-homologous end joining repair, that are usually deletions (Connahs et al., 2019; Mazo-Vargas et al., 2022; Van Belleghem et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about butterfly CRISPR experiments supported by citations.

claim: Regulatory CRISPR-induced alleles should ideally require genotyping in a second (G1) generation to be properly matched to a phenotype.
source: Ideally, regulatory CRISPR-induced alleles should require genotyping in a second (G1) generation to be properly matched to a phenotype (Mazo-Vargas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about best practices in CRISPR experiments supported by a citation.

claim: The authors failed to pass Ubx locus G0 mutations to a G1 generation for genotyping, possibly because of lethal effects.
source: Possibly because of lethal effects, we failed to pass Ubx locus G0 mutations to a G1 generation for genotyping, and were thus limited here to mosaic analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental limitations encountered in this study.

claim: Cas9 nuclease targeting can generate larger than expected mutations that evade common genotyping techniques.
source: Some of these clones may have been the results of large structural variants, as data from other organisms suggests that Cas9 nuclease targeting can generate larger than expected mutations that evade common genotyping techniques (Shin et al., 2017; Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Cullot et al., 2019; Owens et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about CRISPR mutagenesis supported by citations.

claim: Targeting the ATAC-seq peaks with multiple sgRNAs spanning sub-domains 11 a and 11 c yielded dual homeoses: FW➞HW and HW➞FW.
source: Targeting the ATAC-seq peaks with multiple sgRNAs spanning sub-domains 11 a and 11 c (UbxCRE11a2c5 in V. cardui, 11 a2a3c5c6 in J. coenia), or with a single target in 11 c (UbxCRE11c5 in V. cardui) yielded dual homeoses: FW➞HW and HW➞FW (Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Targeting a single target in CRM11 sub-domain 11 c yielded dual homeoses: FW➞HW and HW➞FW.
source: Targeting the ATAC-seq peaks with multiple sgRNAs spanning sub-domains 11 a and 11 c (UbxCRE11a2c5 in V. cardui, 11 a2a3c5c6 in J. coenia), or with a single target in 11 c (UbxCRE11c5 in V. cardui) yielded dual homeoses: FW➞HW and HW➞FW (Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hindwing effects in CRM11 crispants were reminiscent of Ubx protein coding knockouts.
source: Hindwing effects were reminiscent of Ubx protein coding knockouts (Tendolkar et al., 2021), indicating that these crispant alleles with a hindwing phenotype produce Ubx loss-of-function effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes to known Ubx knockouts.

claim: CRM11 crispant alleles with a hindwing phenotype produce Ubx loss-of-function effects.
source: Hindwing effects were reminiscent of Ubx protein coding knockouts (Tendolkar et al., 2021), indicating that these crispant alleles with a hindwing phenotype produce Ubx loss-of-function effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of phenotypes to known Ubx knockouts.

claim: Individuals with hindwing clones were 2.75 times more common than individuals with forewings in the CRM11 dataset.
source: Individuals with hindwing clones were 2.75 times more common than individuals with forewings in this dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data summarized in Figure 9.

claim: Dual homeoses in CRM11 crispants may indicate the presence of hindwing activators and forewing repressors in the CRM11 region.
source: Similarly to the lncRNA loci perturbation experiments, dual homeoses may indicate the presence of hindwing activators and forewing repressors in the CRM11 region, with various CRISPR alleles producing a spectrum of indels and effects (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the bidirectional homeotic phenotypes observed.

claim: Single-target experiments in CRM11 showed little lethality (55% hatching rate).
source: It is noteworthy that while single-target experiments showed little lethality (55% hatching rate), dual or quadruple injection mixes resulted in low hatching rates of injected embryos (~10%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Dual or quadruple injection mixes in CRM11 experiments resulted in low hatching rates of injected embryos (~10%).
source: It is noteworthy that while single-target experiments showed little lethality (55% hatching rate), dual or quadruple injection mixes resulted in low hatching rates of injected embryos (~10%).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Multiple targeting in CRM11 appears to induce high-rates of embryonic lethality, possibly due to chromosomal damage.
source: Multiple targeting thus appears to induce high-rates of embryonic lethality, possibly due to chromosomal damage (Cullot et al., 2019; Zuccaro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed lethality and established knowledge about CRISPR-induced chromosomal damage.

claim: Dual targeting with a2 +c5 in CRM11 yielded partial HW➞FW homeoses in V. cardui under the form of ectopic white eyespot foci phenotypes.
source: Dual targeting with a2 +c5 also yielded partial HW➞FW homeoses in V. cardui under the form of ectopic white eyespot foci phenotypes (Figure 7E), as occasionally observed in Ubx null crispants (Tendolkar et al., 2021), seemingly due to hypomorphic or heterozygous allelic states.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 7E.

claim: Ectopic white eyespot foci phenotypes are occasionally observed in Ubx null crispants.
source: Dual targeting with a2 +c5 also yielded partial HW➞FW homeoses in V. cardui under the form of ectopic white eyespot foci phenotypes (Figure 7E), as occasionally observed in Ubx null crispants (Tendolkar et al., 2021), seemingly due to hypomorphic or heterozygous allelic states.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Region 11b is deeply conserved across 23 lepidopteran species and 2 trichopteran species.
source: A whole genome alignment between 23 lepidopteran species and 2 trichopteran species indicated that region 11b is deeply conserved, suggesting important functional constraints on its sequence (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic conservation analysis presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The deep conservation of region 11b suggests important functional constraints on its sequence.
source: A whole genome alignment between 23 lepidopteran species and 2 trichopteran species indicated that region 11b is deeply conserved, suggesting important functional constraints on its sequence (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed genomic conservation.

claim: Mutagenesis of 11b using a single guide RNA (Ubx11b9) yielded a relatively high hatching rate (mean = 51.8 %).
source: Mutagenesis of 11b using a single guide RNA (Ubx11b9) yielded a relatively high hatching rate (mean = 51.8 %), indicating a rare occurrence of the deleterious mutational effects observed in multiple targeting (see above).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Four J. coenia crispants and two V. cardui crispants targeting Ubx11b9 were obtained, all exclusively showing hindwing phenotype devoid of forewing effects.
source: Four J. coenia crispants and two V. cardui crispants were obtained, all exclusively showing hindwing phenotype devoid of forewing effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: HW➞FW homeoses in Ubx11b9 crispants included a variety of phenotypes all seen in Ubx CDS mutants.
source: HW➞FW homeoses included a variety of phenotypes all seen in Ubx CDS mutants (Tendolkar et al., 2021), including transformations of the orange Discalis elements and the white band in J. coenia, and partial shifts in eyespot identity (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR mutagenesis experiments and phenotypic observations presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The consistency in direction of transformations and the deep conservation of the 11b region suggests it may encode an enhancer necessary for the transcriptional activation of Ubx in hindwings.
source: Together the consistency in direction of transformations and the deep conservation of the 11b region suggests it may encode an enhancer necessary for the transcriptional activation of Ubx in hindwings.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the phenotypic data and genomic conservation.

claim: Homeotic shifts between forewings and hindwings can occur naturally in Lepidoptera.
source: Homeotic shifts between forewings and hindwings can occur naturally in Lepidoptera, and have been documented as pattern aberrations in museum specimens (Sibatani, 1980; Sibatani, 1983).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Across 15 spontaneous mutants in Heliconius, 12 show HW➞FW clones, against 3 specimens with FW➞HW effects.
source: Across these 15 spontaneous mutants, 12 show HW➞FW clones, against 3 specimens with FW➞HW effects (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of spontaneous mutants presented in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Mutant clones in the Heliconius spontaneous mutant dataset were always posterior to the M2 vein.
source: Mutant clones in this dataset were always posterior to the M2 vein.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of spontaneous mutants presented in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Only 2 mosaic phenotypes in the Heliconius spontaneous mutant dataset were found on a dorsal side, with the 13 others appearing ventrally.
source: Only 2 mosaic phenotypes were found on a dorsal side, with the 13 others appearing ventrally.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of spontaneous mutants presented in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Heliconius homeotic mosaics show pattern shifts with complete fore/hindwing conversions of scale types.
source: These homeotic mosaics show pattern shifts with complete fore/hindwing conversions of scale types, as seen for instance in the loss of gray wing coupling scales on posterior ventral forewings (Figure 8A–B), or conversely, in their acquisition in posterior hindwings (arrowheads in Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of spontaneous mutants presented in Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Heliconius homeoses include noticeable local changes in wing shape, particularly in hindwings.
source: Homeoses also include noticeable local changes in wing shape, particularly in hindwings (asterisks in Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of spontaneous mutants presented in Figure 8—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: Fore/hindwing homeotic aberrations found in nature and captive stocks may result from mutations at the Ubx locus itself.
source: Taken together, these effects are akin to CRISPR-induced perturbations at the Ubx locus. We speculate that fore/hindwing homeotic aberrations, found in nature and captive stocks, result from mutations at the Ubx locus itself.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the similarity of spontaneous mutants to CRISPR-induced phenotypes.
